Custom Silicon vs Nvidia: Can the Hyperscalers Break the GPU Monopoly?

Nvidia earns a 75% gross margin selling the chips that run AI, and every one of its biggest customers is now designing its own. Google sells TPUs to rivals, Amazon trains Anthropic's models on Trainium, OpenAI shipped its first chip this year and Broadcom's AI revenue is nearly tripling. This guide explains GPUs versus custom accelerators, profiles every challenger, follows the money through the supply chain, maps where Nvidia's software moat holds and where it is eroding, and lets you test when building your own chip pays off.

The 75% question

In the quarter to 26 July 2026, Nvidia reported revenue of $96.2 billion, up 106% on a year earlier. Its data center business alone brought in $89.0 billion, $48.7 billion of it from the big cloud companies. Its gross margin was 75%: for every dollar a hyperscaler spends on Nvidia hardware, roughly 75 cents is Nvidia's gross profit. It guided to $108 billion for the next quarter and says it expects about 70% revenue growth in its next fiscal year, limited mainly by how many chips it can get made.

That margin is the single biggest reason Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Meta and OpenAI all now design their own AI chips. If you are spending tens of billions of dollars a year on accelerators, capturing even part of that margin is worth a chip team of thousands. Jensen Huang's reply is that building AI infrastructure is "really hard" and most custom chip projects never reach production. Both things can be true.

GPU vs ASIC in plain words

A GPU is a general-purpose parallel processor: thousands of small cores that can run almost any maths, programmed through Nvidia's CUDA software. An ASIC (application-specific integrated circuit) is a chip designed for one kind of job. Google's TPU, Amazon's Trainium and Microsoft's Maia are ASICs built around the matrix multiplications that dominate neural networks. They give up some flexibility to spend more of their silicon, memory and power on exactly that work. Click a point on the spectrum.

The flexibility vs efficiency spectrum

Qualitative positions; real chips blur the lines (Nvidia GPUs contain specialised tensor cores, and TPUs are programmable).

Market share depends on how you count

Ask "how much of the market does Nvidia have?" and you get answers from about 62% to 85%. The gap is mostly method: Nvidia's chips are far more expensive than custom ones, so its share of revenue is much higher than its share of chips shipped.

Nvidia's share of AI accelerators, by estimate

Each bar is a different tracker or measure; none is authoritative. The unit figure comes from a low-authority tracker and is shown as a range midpoint.

The direction is clearer than the level. TrendForce forecast in October 2025 that AI servers built on cloud providers' custom chips would grow 44.6% in 2026, against 16.1% for GPU-based AI servers. Nvidia is still growing very fast in dollars; its share is what is slipping, slowly, at the edges.

Google's TPU story, 2015 to 2026

Google is the only hyperscaler with a decade of custom AI silicon behind it, and in 2026 it took a step none of the others has: selling TPUs to outside companies, including competitors. SemiAnalysis reported that of roughly a million TPUs for Anthropic, about 400,000 Ironwood chips would be sold as finished racks (worth about $10 billion) through Broadcom and about 600,000 rented through Google Cloud. The Information reported that Meta signed a multibillion-dollar lease of TPU capacity with an option to buy Ironwood outright from 2027. Bloomberg reported that Google DeepMind's own researchers are queuing for TPU time as a result.

Follow the money: who designs, who builds, who makes

"Custom" rarely means a company does everything itself. Most hyperscalers design the architecture and hand the rest to a design partner, mainly Broadcom or Marvell, which turns it into a manufacturable chip, adds high-speed interfaces and manages production at TSMC. Broadcom and Marvell together are estimated to hold about 95% of this co-design market. Pick a chip to trace its chain.

AI revenue scale: Nvidia vs Broadcom

US$ billions per year. Nvidia's figure is our annualisation of one quarter's data center revenue (×4); Broadcom's are management guidance and targets.

  • Broadcom reported $8.4 billion of AI semiconductor revenue in its fiscal first quarter of 2026, up 106%. By its third quarter, custom accelerators ("XPUs") were 73% of AI revenue and shipments had more than tripled. It guides to about $58 billion of AI revenue for fiscal 2026, holds a $73 billion AI backlog and says it has "line of sight" to more than $100 billion of AI chip revenue in 2027.
  • Its six custom-chip customers are Google, Meta, Anthropic, OpenAI and two it does not name. It is shipping Google's TPU 8i ahead of the MediaTek-built 8t.
  • Marvell works with Amazon on Trainium and Microsoft on Maia; one source projects up to $11 billion of AI custom-chip revenue for it in 2026.

The CUDA moat, layer by layer

Nvidia's strongest defence is not the chip; it is two decades of software. But "CUDA lock-in" is not one thing. Click each layer of the stack to see where switching away is getting easier and where it is still hard.

Where lock-in lives

Green = eroding, amber = mixed, red = still strong. Summary of practitioner and analyst sources; mostly 2026 blogs, not primary research.

💡 The short version If your team serves models with PyTorch and an engine like vLLM and never wrote custom CUDA, moving to another chip is, in one practitioner's words, "closer to a reinstall than a rewrite". If you train frontier models across thousands of chips with hand-tuned kernels and Nvidia's networking, switching is a multi-year engineering project. That is why custom chips win inference first.

Build vs buy: when does a custom chip pay off?

The basic trade is a large fixed cost (designing the chip and its software) against a lower cost per chip (no Nvidia margin, though a design partner and foundry still take theirs). Whether it pays depends on volume and on how much useful work each custom chip does compared with a GPU.

Build vs buy calculator

All defaults are illustrative assumptions, not reported costs. "Manufacturing cost" is the cost to make one comparable accelerator; the GPU price is derived from it using Nvidia's margin. Ignores networking, software staff over time, power differences and timing.

Play with it and a pattern appears: at tens of thousands of chips, the fixed cost dominates and buying wins; at hundreds of thousands to millions, avoiding the margin dominates and building wins, if the custom chip does comparable work. That is exactly the scale at which Google, Amazon, Meta and OpenAI operate, and why smaller buyers still mostly buy Nvidia.

Why custom chips win inference first

TrainingInference
WorkloadChanges with every research ideaA few known models served billions of times
SoftwareHand-tuned kernels, deep CUDA dependenceStandard frameworks and serving engines; easier to port
NetworkingThousands of chips in lockstep (NCCL, NVLink)Small groups of chips per request
What matters mostTime to result; flexibilityCost per token and power, where specialisation pays
Share of computeAbout one-third in 2026 (Deloitte estimate)About two-thirds, and growing
Who is winningNvidia (Google TPUs the main exception)Custom chips gaining: Maia 200, MTIA, TPU 8i, Trainium all lead with inference

Google's 2026 split of its TPU line into a training chip (8t) and an inference chip (8i) makes the point in hardware. Meta says its MTIA chips have done better at inference than at generative-AI training, and Microsoft's Maia 200 is explicitly an inference accelerator.

Why custom chip programs fail

  • Moving targets. Microsoft's next Maia chip (codenamed Braga) slipped at least six months to 2026 after, according to The Information, OpenAI requested new features late in development, which destabilised the design in simulation.
  • People. The same reporting cited staffing shortages and turnover of up to 20% on some teams under deadline pressure. Chip teams are scarce and poached constantly.
  • Architecture drift. A chip takes two to three years from design to deployment; model architectures change faster. A chip tuned for last year's models can miss this year's (mixture-of-experts, long context, new number formats).
  • Training is harder than inference. Meta, by Reuters' account, has had more success with inference chips than with a generative-AI training chip.
  • You still need partners. Custom does not escape Broadcom's or Marvell's margins, TSMC's capacity or the HBM shortage (see The Memory Wall).
  • Software is the real cost. Compilers, kernels, debugging tools and framework support take as long as the silicon, and keep costing money every generation.

Nvidia strikes back

Nvidia's counter-moves

Three scenarios to 2030

🟢 Nvidia holds ~80% of revenue

Frontier training stays on Nvidia, new architectures keep outrunning ASICs, and Nvidia's yearly cadence and system integration (chips, networking, software) keep it ahead. Custom chips settle into each hyperscaler's own inference. Signal: Nvidia's gross margin stays above 70%.

🟡 A 60/40 split

Inference, two-thirds of compute and rising, moves heavily to TPUs, Trainium, Maia, MTIA and OpenAI's chips; Nvidia keeps training and the long tail of customers. Analyst forecasts of 10–25% custom-silicon share by 2028–2030 sit at the low end of this. Signal: Broadcom hits its $100B+ 2027 target.

🔴 Commoditisation

Framework-level portability makes accelerators interchangeable, Google sells TPUs widely, AMD's racks compete on price, and margins fall toward ordinary chip levels. Signal: frontier labs train flagship models off Nvidia; Nvidia margin below 60%.

🧭 Closing

🎯 The bottom line Nvidia is not losing; it is growing faster than almost any company of its size ever has. But its share is no longer a law of nature. Every company big enough to buy a million chips now builds some of its own, starting with inference, where the workload is stable and the software is portable, and Google has gone further by selling TPUs to rivals. Nvidia's defences are real: frontier training, networking, the deepest software stack and a punishing release cadence. The likeliest future is not a collapse but a split: Nvidia for training and the long tail, custom silicon for the biggest buyers' inference, and margins that slowly come down. Watch Broadcom's 2027 revenue and Nvidia's gross margin.
